title: Vietnam abolishes death penalty for drug trafficking, leaving four capital offences
summary: Vietnam's National Assembly has voted to remove the death penalty for drug trafficking and five other crimes, leaving execution available for only four offences in a landmark narrowing of capital punishment.
content:
Vietnam has abolished the death penalty for drug trafficking and five other crimes, in the most significant narrowing of capital punishment in the country's modern history. The National Assembly passed a revised Penal Code on Friday, November 20, leaving execution available as a punishment for only four offences.

Under the new code, capital punishment will be reserved for treason, murder, terrorism and the illegal production of narcotics. Drug trafficking, the rape of a person under 16, rioting, crimes against humanity, war crimes and terrorism aimed at opposing the people's government will no longer carry the death penalty, with life imprisonment becoming the maximum sentence instead, according to [Channel News Asia](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/asia/vietnam-death-penalty-abolish-crime-6571011).

The vote was decisive. The revised code, which contains 417 articles across 25 chapters, was approved by 463 of the 472 deputies present, according to Vietnamese media. It takes effect on March 1, 2027, with a separate resolution on how to implement it scheduled to take effect on December 3, 2026.

The change will also reach backwards. Prisoners already sentenced to death for the six offences who have not yet been executed will have their sentences commuted to life imprisonment, Vietnamese media reported. And the new sentencing rules will apply to trials held on or after the effective date, even when the alleged offence took place earlier — meaning a person accused of trafficking drugs before March 2027 could not receive a death sentence in a trial held after the new law takes effect.

The decision did not pass without argument. During deliberations, some lawmakers voiced reservations about removing capital punishment for drug trafficking, a serious offence in a country that sits on major regional trafficking routes, and about the rape of children under 16. Minister of Public Security Luong Tam Quang defended the change in the Assembly, arguing that there is no convincing basis to show that the death penalty deters drug crime more effectively than life imprisonment. The government also drew a deliberate distinction between trafficking and production: making drugs remains a capital offence, while moving them no longer is, reflecting what officials described as a difference in the nature and danger of the two crimes.

Legal experts in Hanoi welcomed the vote as a milestone. Dr Dang Van Cuong, a criminal lawyer and lecturer at Thuy Loi University, told Vietnamese media that narrowing the scope of the death penalty, gradually reducing it and eventually abolishing it, is an inevitable trend in criminal policy, and described the decision as a step that clearly demonstrates the humane nature of Vietnam's criminal policy.

The vote continues a long, slow retreat from capital punishment that began decades ago. Vietnam's 1985 Penal Code listed 44 crimes that could attract the death penalty. Successive revisions cut that number to 10, and Friday's vote brings it down to four. The direction of travel is now unmistakable, even if full abolition remains a distant prospect in a country where the ruling Communist Party has traditionally treated harsh punishment as a pillar of public order.

The move also sets Vietnam apart from some of its neighbours. Singapore still executes drug traffickers, and Malaysia only abolished the mandatory death penalty for drug offences in 2023, replacing it with judicial discretion. Vietnam's decision to remove the offence from the capital list entirely goes further than either, and it comes as the country seeks to present itself as a modernising, rules-based economy open to foreign investment and deeper integration with the West.

Human rights groups have long ranked Vietnam among the world's most active users of the death penalty, though the government treats execution figures as a state secret and does not publish them. Campaigners have argued for years that the secrecy itself is part of the problem, making it impossible to know how many people are on death row or how the punishment is applied. Friday's vote does not end executions in Vietnam, but it will sharply reduce the number of people who can be sentenced to death, and it gives those already condemned for the six offences a reprieve they did not expect.

The timing is notable. The vote came the same week that Vietnam's parliament also passed a law speeding up land expropriation for priority infrastructure projects, and a day after leaders from the United States, Russia and China met in Shenzhen in a [first-of-its-kind trilateral summit](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/xi-trump-putin-summit-shenzhen-november-19) hosted by President Xi Jinping. For a country that has spent the past decade balancing its relationships with Washington, Beijing and Moscow, the penal code vote is a reminder that some of its most consequential decisions are still domestic ones.

What happens next will be watched closely. The implementation resolution due in December will set out how courts handle cases already in the system, and the March 2027 start date gives prosecutors and judges time to adjust. The bigger question is whether the narrowing stops at four offences or becomes a step towards abolition. For now, the government has framed the change as a careful, gradual reform — a phrase that, in Vietnam's politics, usually means the direction is set but the destination is not yet fixed. For the prisoners whose death sentences will now be commuted, however, the destination hardly matters. The law has already changed their lives.
